title: The fast before the crowning
hookLine: the king rushes the crowning to tomorrow, and Rama and Sita spend the night fasting on sacred grass
carry: upavasa: a fast is staying near

cards: Tonight's story has two kinds of waiting in it. One is an old king who can't wait: the assembly has said yes, and now he wants it done by morning.

The other is a young couple told how to wait well: a fast, a bath, an offering, and a night on sacred grass before a pouring at dawn. Hindus still keep that second kind of night before a big puja or a holy day.

teach.b: First Rama comes to his father's hall, bows, and hears the news in public. Rama goes home. Then the charioteer Sumantra comes back for him: the king wants you again.
This time Dasharatha speaks privately, and he sounds afraid.
I've had bad dreams. Meteors have fallen with a crash. The astrologers say my star is under pressure from harsh planets.
So the coronation will be tomorrow. Then he says something honest, and a little chilling.

teach.h: DO IT WHILE BHARATA IS AWAY.
teach.b: Do it now, while Bharata is away. Bharata is good, he says, devoted to his elder brother. But the minds of people change, even good people.
The king isn't accusing anyone. He's admitting he doesn't trust time.
Then he tells Rama what the night requires, and the priest Vasishtha comes to see it done: tonight you and Sita keep a fast, and sleep on the ground, on a bed of sacred kusha grass.
Rama and Sita bathe, make an offering, and spend the night quietly in a shrine. Here's the teaching inside that night. The word is upavasa, a fast.
Upa means near; vasa, staying. Many teachers read it just that way: a fast isn't a punishment, it's a way of staying near God, setting the plate aside so the mind has room.
It's the same spirit in which Hindus still fast on Ekadashi, on Shivaratri, or before a family puja, and it's why a prince sleeps on grass instead of a bed tonight.

teach.h: A COUPLE STAYING NEAR. A KING IN A HURRY.
teach.b: So two kinds of waiting sit side by side tonight: a couple staying near, and a king who wants it finished before his own son can come home.

how: Fasting and keeping vigil the night before a major rite is a common Hindu practice, on days like Ekadashi and Shivaratri and before family pujas; in the text, Dasharatha and then Vasishtha tell Rama and Sita to fast and sleep on kusha grass before the consecration.

o: a feast held the night before a coronation
a fast kept the night before a sacred rite
a prayer spoken by the king's astrologers

games.q: the night before — tap the pairs.
p: part of the king's bad omens
tells Rama and Sita to fast

s: its parts mean near and staying; many teachers read a fast as a way of staying near God.
the king moves the coronation to the next day
he's shaken by bad dreams and omens.
Rama and Sita spend the night feasting
they fast and sleep on sacred grass, as Vasishtha instructs.

games.q: you're Rama, the night before the rite. Vasishtha tells you and Sita how to spend it. what does he ask?
o: fast, and sleep on sacred grass.
feast with the city until dawn.
games.why: they fast, bathe, make an offering and sleep on kusha grass in a shrine: upavasa, a night of staying near.

practice: Sit the way Rama and Sita sat that night, low and quiet. If you pray, repeat a name you love, Rama, Shiva, or simply om, on each breath out, and let that be the whole sit.
If you don't pray, sit with the breath, and when the urge comes to reach for a snack or your phone, let it remind you to come back. That's upavasa, small: staying near instead of filling up.

wordCard.voice: Upavasa, the fast Rama and Sita keep the night before the rite. Upa, near; vasa, staying: a fast read as staying close to God.

orig.note: Sanskrit upavāsa: a fast, literally staying near. Rama and Sita keep one the night before the rite.

carryVoice: Your line: upavasa, a fast is staying near. Rama and Sita kept the night quiet, while the king rushed. Day five hundred fifteen, done.
